Long Covid: Lessons from ME/CFS

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
ME/CFS has long been a source of mystery, but efforts directed at understanding Long Covid might at last reveal the cause of this debilitating syndrome and - possibly - a cure.

Unique Selling Point:
Long Covid is a new medical phenomenon and is still greeted with cynicism by some in the scientific community. Similarly, those suffering the debilitating effects of ME/CFS struggled to convince doctors that their symptoms - utterly life-changing in most cases - were real. But scientific skepticism isn't the only thing these two syndromes have in common: they also share a remarkable number of symptoms such as brain fog, joint pain and a malaise that follows even slight physical exertion. Is it possible Long Covid could lead to ME/CFS in some patients? And, does their similarity reveal how Long Covid should be treated? With huge resources being poured into understanding Long Covid, could ME/CFS benefit from those studies?

Summary:
There's ongoing research about what causes ME/CFS, but most experts are of the view that it’s a genetic disease triggered by something that puts stress on the immune system, like a viral infection. Even in its mildest forms, it can leave people exhausted from the most mundane of activities like taking a shower or a short walk. Severe cases are often bed-ridden and unable to talk. ‘Long Covid’ or ‘Post-Covid Syndrome’ is causing similar levels of debate having left a lot of doctors scratching their heads.

Because of their similarities scientists are asking whether ‘Long Covid’ that meets certain diagnostic criteria and lasts for longer than 6 months, is in fact ME/CFSs. Professor Ron Davis, a Stanford geneticist whose son has very severe ME/CFS, told CNN recently that some Covid Long Haulers do have ME/CFS. Others are urging more caution and further research.
What is clear – and a potential game-changer - is that people living with the chronic symptoms of ME/CFS (for so long ignored and misunderstood, their condition under-researched) will likely benefit from the work going into understanding ‘Long Covid’.
This story will examine the link/similarities between ‘Long Covid’ and ME/CFS by re-telling the story of Retha Viviers, founder of the ME/CFS Foundation of South Africa, who continues to fight the cause of those living with ME/CFS. Her advocacy now includes a keen interest in the research on the link with ‘Long Covid’. It will also include an updated interview with Prof Davis and several other researchers currently involved in finding answers to the complex questions: “Is Long Covid actually ME/CFS or a different type of post-infection syndrome?” and “Will global attempts at understanding Long Covid deliver a long-awaited treatment or even cure for ME/CFS?”. ENDS

Script:


VO: Not long after the start of the Covid19 pandemic, reports emerged of people battling persistent symptoms after recovering from their initial illness. They became known as “Long Haulers” and included people who’d only suffered mild or moderate disease.

Link: Long Covid or Post-Covid Syndrome: At its worst, it can leave those who’ve cleared the virus suffering a long list of symptoms including extreme fatigue, insomnia, depression and what’s known as brain fog.

VO: In fact, according to some reports, there are at least 50 different symptoms associated with Long Covid.

Upsound Dr Ngoepe [03:34 – 03:42] I started getting shortness of breath, struggling with chest pain, getting an unbelievable level of fatigue

Link: We were introduced to Dr. Pheidah Ngoepe late last year when she appeared in our story on so called Covid Long Haulers. Having contracted the virus while on the medical frontline, she was still battling debilitating symptoms months later.

UPSOUND Dr Ngoepe [03:50 to 04:00]: “Now, I can’t do much, I can’t even go to the grocery store to buy my own groceries because I physically can’t carry it.

VO: Estimates vary, but a British survey found one in 10 people who tested positive for Covid-19 still had symptoms months later. A significant global effort is now underway to try and figure out why. That’s encouraging news: and not just for those with Long Covid.

Retha Upsound [00:00:00:09 - 00:00:33:03] I woke up in a lot of pain that I took some painkillers. So, yeah, I'm ready for action…

VO: The past few years have not always been kind to Retha Viviers: diagnosed with stage 4 Cancer in early 2020, she’s also one of around 20 million people worldwide living with Myalgic encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome. She founded South Africa’s ME/CFS Foundation and, despite her own challenges, continues to offer valuable advice and support to that community. At its worst, ME/CFS can leave people bed-ridden, unable to speak or feed themselves. Its exact cause is unknown, although it often follows viral infections, and it has no established treatments or cure. While Retha has a mild form, a 2017 interview with Carte Blanche still offered a glimpse of how life changing this complex illness can be.

Retha Viviers Archive upsound [07:19 – 07:26] “Comparing ME tiredness to other people’s tiredness is like comparing a match to an atom bomb”

VO: 13 years since her ME/CFS diagnosis, fatigue remains a constant presence.

ITV: Retha Viviers [00:02:06:03 - 00:02:28:11] I know I can drive short distances. I know I need to rest every three-and-a-half hours for an hour. I know I can't do more than one visit today. If I go to the shops, I know I can’t do something else the rest of the day.

VO: Fatigue is a core symptom of ME/CFS. Another, which can follow even light physical or mental activity, is called Post Exertional Malaise – simply referred to as the “crash”.

ITV Retha Viviers [00:02:41:19 - 00:03:20:09] STRAP “Founder: ME/CFS Foundations SA” It's absolutely as if you feel like you're going to die, you have zero energy, feel ill. It's not like “I'm tired, I need to go lie down for a bit. No, you absolutely feel completely ill from that crash.

VO: From fatigue and sleep trouble to impaired memory, the list of potential ME/CFS symptoms is varied. But there’s a striking similarity to those endured by people with Long Covid. So, are these similar but distinct conditions? Or is there an overlap suggesting something far more significant? An organisation in the U.S. believes a large subset of people with Long Covid will inevitably be diagnosed with ME/CFS.

UPSOUND DEREK [Justin Cam Clip 44, 17:35 – 17:38] “Linda great to meet you, my name’s Derek”.

VO: Linda Tannenbaum is Founder of Open Medicine Foundation which she established to help fund and facilitate research into ME/CFS.
Derek Watts Question: What were your first thoughts when you heard the reports of long covid?

ITV Linda Tannenbaum [00:07:36:05 - 00:08:18:00] STRAP “Founder: Open Medicine Foundation” since the majority of people develop ME/CFS from an initial infection, I was really afraid (CUT) that so many more people would get ME/CFS after getting covid. 00:08:37:17 - 00:09:07:19 So I actually started hearing from more and more people that had Post Covid symptoms that were approaching us and asking, “I think I have this disease that you're studying”.

VO: It’s not unusual for symptoms to linger after viral and other infections: this paper mentions 13. But the current pandemic is still unfolding, and the scale of its post viral potential isn’t fully understood. Tannenbaum is concerned.

ITV Linda Tannenbaum [00:09:07:22 - 00:09:15:23] We have no idea how many people are really sick with this. It really is like a second pandemic.

VO: While a Covid infection has led to symptoms that last for several weeks in a large number of people, ME/CFS is generally only diagnosed when symptoms persist for longer than six months. This opinion paper conservatively predicts the Covid pandemic will cause the number of people with ME/CFS to grow by 10 million globally by the end of this year. A disheartening number when you consider that the lives of only about 5% of people with ME/CFS ever return to normal.

ITV Ron Tompkins [00:17:23:11 - 00:17:54:08] there will be individuals whose various tissues never fully recover (CUT)

VO: Dr. Ron Tompkins is Chief Medical Officer at Open Medicine Foundation.

ITV Ron Tompkins [00:17:23:11 - 00:17:54:08] And it can be in your lungs, heart, central nervous system, your brain. But some tissues just simply fail to return to normal.

Derek Watts [00:17:55:05 - 00:17:57:07] And that remains a mystery.

ITV Ron Tompkins [00:17:58:09 - 00:17:59:17] It's totally a mystery.

VO: “Mystery” is a word often associated with ME/CFS, not least because the disease still lacks a standard, reliable diagnostic test.

ITV Ron Tompkins [00:18:05:15 - 00:18:49:07] STRAP “Harvard Medical School and Open Medicine Foundation” one of the terrible conundrums in ME/CFS is the fact that you have these terrible symptoms, yet all the tests that the typical clinician would do return normal. The images, the biomarkers become normal, yet the patients continue to suffer from this terrible fatigue and inability to function.

VO: Relying on symptoms alone to make a diagnosis means ME/CFS was - and often still is - seen as an imagined disease.

ITV Ron Tompkins [00:23:31:12 - 00:24:12:19] the seriousness of ME/CFS is grossly underplayed, under recognized. I've found in the United States that many of our institutions have a bias that is in total denial of this disease.

VO: For Tompkins and like-minded researchers, it’s imperative people with Long Covid don’t encounter similar indifference – especially those whose symptoms suggest ME/CFS.
Ron Davis ITV [00:30:50:19 - 00:31:27:06] government agencies really need to take MECFS seriously. It's not a fraud, it's not an imaginary disease, it's a real disease, and it's pretty much lifelong.

VO: Dr Ron Davis, who also featured in our 2017 story, knows that all too well. His son, Whitney Dafoe, has a severe form of the disease and requires constant care. A renowned geneticist, Dr Davis has been single-minded in trying to help his son and others like him.

ITV Ron Davis [00:13:27:20 - 00:14:21:10 ] STRAP “Director: Open Medicine Foundation Scientific Advisory Board” I believe this disease is curable because patients do get over this. It's rare, but they do get over it. And when they do get over it, they're totally normal. They don't have any of the symptoms at all. So if they can spontaneously get over it, we should be able to do something that pushes them in that direction and their normal.

VO: But he too worries past mistakes in dealing with ME/CFS will be repeated during and after this pandemic. One of the most controversial was a study that found patients benefitted from exercise and psychological therapy – something Dr. Davis and other ME/CFS activists strongly reject. And with the U.S. Congress alone making more than a billion dollars available over four years to study Long Covid, a good way of avoiding those mistakes is leaning on the ME/CFS research community.

ITV Ron Davis [00:21:23:12 - 00:21:45:02] it would be really good to have some joint effort and it would be really good if some of the long hauler funding actually funded ME/CFS because there's a long history of work there that the community would benefit from instead of starting from scratch.

ITV Linda Tannenbaum [00:12:00:13 - 00:12:27:07] We're insisting our government includes ME/CFS in the post covid research agenda because there is a lot of money on the table to study post-Covid Syndrome. This is so important and basically, if not now, when? Now's our chance to really scale up the research.

Link - For years, people living with ME/CFS have had to battle the tide of scepticism and even indifference towards a disease that has so dramatically changed their lives. And it’s taken a pandemic to give them renewed hope for a diagnostic test, viable treatments or even a cure.

VO: The irony isn’t lost on Retha Viviers, but, far from bitter, she’s more determined than ever to fight her community’s cause.

ITV Retha Viviers [00:05:35:07 - 00:06:08:03] STRAP “Founder ME/CFS Foundation SA” the moment we started seeing that there was a problem after a few months with the COVID patients, we just came to the party and started advocating educating them. Well, the patients, the doctors and saying, “please, people, listen to your bodies. We have the knowledge. We have learned the hard way”. And instead of being bitter that we didn't get that attention, we said, “now let's help you guys. You are our brothers and sisters in this.”
ENDS>

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ME/CFS has long been a source of mystery, but efforts directed at understanding Long Covid might at last reveal the cause of this debilitating syndrome and - possibly - a cure.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Long Covid is a new medical phenomenon and is still greeted with cynicism by some in the scientific community. Similarly, those suffering the debilitating effects of ME/CFS struggled to convince doctors that their symptoms - utterly life-changing in most cases - were real. But scientific skepticism isn't the only thing these two syndromes have in common: they also share a remarkable number of symptoms such as brain fog, joint pain and a malaise that follows even slight physical exertion. Is it possible Long Covid could lead to ME/CFS in some patients? And, does their similarity reveal how Long Covid should be treated? With huge resources being poured into understanding Long Covid, could ME/CFS benefit from those studies?
metadata.Summary: There's ongoing research about what causes ME/CFS, but most experts are of the view that it’s a genetic disease triggered by something that puts stress on the immune system, like a viral infection. Even in its mildest forms, it can leave people exhausted from the most mundane of activities like taking a shower or a short walk. Severe cases are often bed-ridden and unable to talk. ‘Long Covid’ or ‘Post-Covid Syndrome’ is causing similar levels of debate having left a lot of doctors scratching their heads. Because of their similarities scientists are asking whether ‘Long Covid’ that meets certain diagnostic criteria and lasts for longer than 6 months, is in fact ME/CFSs. Professor Ron Davis, a Stanford geneticist whose son has very severe ME/CFS, told CNN recently that some Covid Long Haulers do have ME/CFS. Others are urging more caution and further research. What is clear – and a potential game-changer - is that people living with the chronic symptoms of ME/CFS (for so long ignored and misunderstood, their condition under-researched) will likely benefit from the work going into understanding ‘Long Covid’. This story will examine the link/similarities between ‘Long Covid’ and ME/CFS by re-telling the story of Retha Viviers, founder of the ME/CFS Foundation of South Africa, who continues to fight the cause of those living with ME/CFS. Her advocacy now includes a keen interest in the research on the link with ‘Long Covid’. It will also include an updated interview with Prof Davis and several other researchers currently involved in finding answers to the complex questions: “Is Long Covid actually ME/CFS or a different type of post-infection syndrome?” and “Will global attempts at understanding Long Covid deliver a long-awaited treatment or even cure for ME/CFS?”. ENDS
